walkthroughs.body_html:
Religion, Philosophy & Ethics: Relationships & Families — a core area of GCSE Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Religion, Philosophy & Ethics: Relationships & Families brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Religion, Philosophy & Ethics: Relationships & Families.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

Is the Buddha a god in Buddhism?
options: Buddhists worship the Buddha as their god.
The ontological argument is the same as the cosmological argument.
The Buddha created the universe.

No — the Buddha (Siddhartha Gautama) is regarded as an enlightened human teacher who discovered the path to liberation. Theravada Buddhism is generally non-theistic; some Mahayana traditions develop more elaborate cosmologies.

mcqs.q: How did Hume define a miracle?
options: The ontological argument is the same as the cosmological argument.
Hume defined a miracle as something amazing or unexpected.
A violation of the laws of nature by a particular volition of the Deity — and he argued evidence for such violations could never outweigh the uniform experience supporting the laws.
Hume believed all miracles in the Bible really happened.

mcqs.q: What is distinctive about the ontological argument?
options: The ontological argument uses scientific evidence to prove God exists.
It tries to prove God's existence purely from the concept of God — a priori reasoning needing no empirical evidence about the world.
The Buddha created the universe.
The ontological argument is the same as the cosmological argument.
